intro: Read the deck for the frameworks and these notes for how to use them. Each note explains why a slide matters, gives you a way to remember it and warns where campaigns slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions cold, and add your own cases in the margins.

sections.title: What Advocacy Is
sections.big_idea: Advocacy is the deliberate effort to **shift who decides and how**, so public systems work for excluded people.
in_plain_words: Service delivery asks how to meet a need. Advocacy asks why the need exists, who decided it would be this way and what rule would have to change. Both are legitimate, but they pull different levers, so advocacy needs its own strategy, timeline and indicators. The slides define four targets: policy, practice, power and norms.

The case for advocacy is scale. An NGO can run 50 schools well, but only a policy and budget shift reaches 5,000 government schools. Words matter as well. Lobbying is one narrow tactic, campaigning a sustained push, activism a style. **The most durable advocacy** is led by the people affected, with NGOs, coalitions, researchers and insiders each adding a piece.

diagram.caption: four targets, from years to a generation

key_terms.meaning: A planned process to influence policy, practice, power and norms.
Meeting a need directly for individuals and communities.
Direct, private communication with officials about a specific decision.
A sustained, public, time-bound push.
Visible action to demand change, often confrontational.
A sympathetic official or reformer within the system.

worked_example.title: Why service alone cannot scale
steps: An NGO runs 50 schools well.
There are 5,000 government schools short of teachers.
The NGO's share is 50 ÷ 5,000 = 1%.
The remaining 99% can only be reached by a policy and budget shift.
So the NGO's schools are most valuable as evidence for a policy ask.
worked_example.answer: The NGO covers 1% of the schools, so the model is best used as evidence for the policy ask.

mistakes: Treating advocacy as what communications does after the programme. It needs its own strategy and indicators.
Using lobbying, campaigning and activism as synonyms. They are different tools within one field.
Winning a law and stopping. Adoption and implementation are separate fights.
Ignoring norms. A policy that runs against prevailing norms is reversed once attention moves.

recall.q: What are the four targets of advocacy?
recall.a: Policy, practice, power and norms.

recall.q: What does advocacy ask that service delivery does not?
recall.a: Why the need exists, who decided it, what rule would have to change and whose voice is missing.

recall.q: What is lobbying, precisely?
recall.a: Direct, private communication with legislators or officials to influence a specific law, rule, budget line or decision.

recall.q: Why is advocacy chronically underfunded?
recall.a: It is harder to report, riskier to be associated with and impossible to claim solely.

recall.q: What does each actor bring to a coalition?
recall.a: Communities bring legitimacy, NGOs reach and evidence, coalitions numbers, researchers and media credibility, insiders timing.

sections.title: Types & Approaches
sections.big_idea: Pick the approach to fit target, power, risk and moment, then **sequence and combine** insider and outsider work.
in_plain_words: Advocacy runs on two tracks. Insiders work quietly through consultations and technical inputs, and outsiders apply public pressure through protest, media and litigation. The strongest campaigns do both, often through different organisations. The four broad approaches are lobbying, campaigning, litigation and mobilisation, and they trade speed against durability.

Questions of voice sit alongside. Advocacy WITH puts affected people in charge, and advocacy FOR speaks on their behalf. The principle 'nothing about us without us' asks who gave you a mandate. MKSS and the RTI movement show the full sequence: **mobilisation, evidence, campaign, law**. Choose by asking what moves the target and who bears the risk.

left.title: Insider
items: Works when the target is willing but constrained

right.title: Outsider
items: Works when the target is unwilling

key_terms.meaning: Public Interest Litigation: courts enforce rights for those who cannot reach them.
A public hearing where records are read against people's testimony.
Public verification of programme records by those affected.
Being absorbed by the system you are trying to change.
Affected people set the agenda, lead and speak.
Authorisation from the affected community to speak for them.

worked_example.title: Sequence an illustrative campaign
worked_example.setup: A coalition wants a state to fill teacher vacancies. Apply the deck's sequencing advice. The case is illustrative.
steps: Mobilise parents and teachers to build a constituency.
Campaign publicly to create pressure on the department.
Lobby the officials and the finance department to close the ask.
Hold litigation in reserve, and use it only if the route shuts.
Each stage makes the next one cheaper.
worked_example.answer: Mobilise, campaign, lobby, then litigate if the route closes.

mistakes: Mistaking being heard for being heeded. In the insider track, being consulted can be the concession.
Filing a case before any engagement. It forecloses the cheaper options.
Treating a judgment as the end. It starts an implementation fight.
Speaking for affected people by default. Use advocacy FOR only where speaking out is unsafe, on their terms.

recall.q: Why does the insider and outsider pairing work?
recall.a: The insider can say 'I cannot control them', and the outside pressure makes the insider's offer look reasonable.

recall.q: What is the trade-off between lobbying and mobilisation?
recall.a: Lobbying is fast but easily reversed, mobilisation is slowest but most durable.

recall.q: What did MKSS's sequence show?
recall.a: Mobilisation generated evidence, evidence fuelled a campaign, the campaign won a law and the law became a permanent tool.

recall.q: What is the honest test of advocacy WITH?
recall.a: What the community can do next year that it could not do last year.

recall.q: What four questions match an approach to the situation?
recall.a: The target, your power, the risk and the moment.

sections.title: Understanding Power
sections.big_idea: Advocacy is applied power analysis. **Diagnose which face of power you face** before choosing a tactic.
in_plain_words: Every advocacy problem is a question of who has power, how it works and how it can shift. Lukes describes three faces: winning open decisions, keeping issues off the table, and shaping what people want. The deeper the face, the less visible the conflict. A tactic suited to one face is wasted on another.

VeneKlasen and Miller split power into over, with, to and within. Only power over is zero-sum, and advocacy builds the other three. Gaventa's power cube adds three axes: spaces, places and forms. **Naming invisible power is itself advocacy**, and a campaign can lose a policy fight yet leave a community more organised than it found it.

levels.label: 1st face: decisions
levels.sub: visible: you lose a fair fight

levels.label: 2nd face: agenda
levels.sub: hidden: you never get the fight

diagram.caption: power gets harder to see as you go down

key_terms.meaning: Lukes: decision-making, agenda-setting and shaping desires.
Control or domination, the power advocacy seeks to change.
Collective strength and solidarity.
Self-worth and dignity, the root of voice.
Decisions made behind shut doors.
A consultation you are asked into, with a tokenism risk.

worked_example.title: Diagnose the face of power
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's symptom table on three situations.
steps: A vote or allocation went against you: first face, so build more power or find a better forum.
You cannot get a meeting, agenda slot or hearing: second face, so force the agenda with media, events or litigation.
The affected people themselves see no problem: third face, so start with consciousness-raising and reframing.
worked_example.answer: First face, second face, third face, each with a different counter-tactic.

mistakes: Lobbying someone who has no authority to deliver. Test with a small ask first.
Using a lobbying strategy on a second-face problem. There is no meeting at which to lobby.
Counting only policy wins. A lost campaign that leaves a community organised is a real result.
Reading an invitation as influence. Ask what changed after the last consultation.

recall.q: What are Lukes' three faces of power?
recall.a: Decision-making, agenda-setting and shaping desires.

recall.q: Which expression of power is zero-sum?
recall.a: Power over.

recall.q: What are the three axes of the power cube?
recall.a: Spaces (closed, invited, claimed), places (local, national, global) and forms (visible, hidden, invisible).

recall.q: How do the forms of power map onto Lukes?
recall.a: Visible is the first face, hidden the second and invisible the third.

recall.q: What is the trap in an invited space?
recall.a: Tokenism: you are consulted and then ignored.

sections.title: The Advocacy Cycle
sections.big_idea: Advocacy is a loop with five stages. **Skipping a stage** is how effort ends up pointed at the wrong target.
in_plain_words: The cycle has five stages: research, strategy, action, monitoring and learning. It loops because the political world moves: a minister is replaced, a window opens, and an eighteen-month-old plan addresses a situation that no longer exists. Each stage has a characteristic failure when rushed.

Research covers evidence about the problem and power analysis about the decision. Strategy names objectives, targets and tactics. Action is the visible part, but its success was decided earlier. Monitoring tracks intermediate signals, and learning feeds the answers back. **Landmark changes took years of cycles**, so build endurance into funding, staffing and morale.

key_terms.meaning: Research on who decides and what moves them.
An early signal that change is under way.
An explicit account of how activities lead to change.
Evidence captured at the time, dated.
Learning fast between rounds and changing course.
A brief opening when change becomes possible.

worked_example.title: Which stage was skipped?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's table of skipped stages on two campaigns.
steps: Campaign A is busy and visible but has no plan: strategy was skipped.
Campaign B tracks only the final ask: monitoring was skipped.
Campaign A's consequence is being busy and ineffective.
Campaign B's consequence is not knowing it is failing until it fails.
worked_example.answer: A skipped strategy and B skipped monitoring.

mistakes: Going straight to a march. The slide says activity can substitute for a plan.
Tracking only the final ask. Intermediate markers show whether the theory of change works.
Reconstructing markers at evaluation time. They are unverifiable by then.
Hiding a failed assumption. It is the most valuable output of a cycle.

recall.q: What are the five stages of the cycle?
recall.a: Research, strategy, action, monitoring and learning.

recall.q: Why does the cycle loop?
recall.a: The political world moves, so each round should reshape the next strategy.

recall.q: What is the cheapest research and most often skipped?
recall.a: What has been tried before, and why it failed.

recall.q: What is the most reliable early signal?
recall.a: An opponent responding publicly to your campaign.

recall.q: How long did RTI take to reach statute?
recall.a: About a decade.

sections.title: Problem & Issue Framing
sections.big_idea: You advocate on issues. **Cut a winnable issue** out of the big problem and frame it for the audience you need.
in_plain_words: A problem is big and structural, like child malnutrition. An issue is a specific, solvable slice with a decision-maker, like filling 200 vacant anganwadi posts. Root-cause analysis, asking 'but why?', finds a rule someone can change. The problem tree shows effects as branches, the core problem as the trunk and causes as roots.

The ask is the concrete action you want a named person to take. It should be specific, winnable, timebound, attributable and meaningful, and set at a stretch that is credible. Framing then decides who supports it: need or right, dignity or cost. **Frame without distortion**, because credibility is the one asset you cannot rebuild quickly.

diagram.caption: frame from the branches, aim at the roots

key_terms.meaning: A specific, solvable slice of a problem with a decision-maker.
The cause you reach by asking 'but why?' repeatedly.
The concrete thing you want a named decision-maker to do.
Choosing which aspect, values and storyline to emphasise.
Presenting a need as an entitlement the state must honour.
Effects as branches, core problem as trunk, causes as roots.

worked_example.title: Track a 200-post ask
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's example of 200 vacant anganwadi posts. The number filled is illustrative.
steps: The district has 200 vacant posts.
Suppose 120 are filled by March.
Posts still vacant are 200 − 120 = 80.
Share filled is 120 ÷ 200 = 60%.
The ask is specific and timebound, so progress is easy to judge.
worked_example.answer: 80 posts remain vacant and 60% were filled by March.

mistakes: Campaigning on a problem. Nobody can grant 'end malnutrition'.
Asking 'why' past the point of a changeable rule. Deeper causes are true but beyond your reach.
Letting the ask become a paragraph. It will be granted in the part that costs least.
Omitting inconvenient context. That is where framing turns into distortion.

recall.q: What is the test of an issue?
recall.a: A named decision-maker can take the action asked for.

recall.q: What are the five tests of a good ask?
recall.a: Specific, winnable, timebound, attributable and meaningful.

recall.q: What calibration do you want for an ask?
recall.a: Difficult but not impossible: the official engages and says it is difficult.

recall.q: What does rights framing change?
recall.a: A beneficiary becomes a claimant, with the state obliged and somewhere to go when refused.

recall.q: What is the framing test?
recall.a: Would the framing survive a hostile public fact-check?

sections.title: Stakeholder & Power Mapping
sections.big_idea: Map the players before you choose tactics. **Move people one step**, and ask who is affected but absent.
in_plain_words: Mapping identifies everyone who affects or is affected by your issue. The four roles are targets who can grant the ask, allies who share the goal, opponents who resist and influentials whom targets listen to. The question maps omit is who is affected but absent. Redo the map each cycle because officials transfer and allies shift.

Lakey's spectrum runs from active allies to active opponents, and the goal is to move each group one step. The highest-return move is turning passive allies into active ones. A support-influence matrix tells you whether to partner, persuade, inform or monitor. **Understand opponents and organise coalitions** by settling roles, decision rules and what happens on a partial win.

key_terms.meaning: The person or body who can grant your ask.
Someone the target listens to.
Lakey's range from active ally to active opponent.
Grid plotting each stakeholder's influence against support.
Someone who agrees and does nothing.
A partial offer that can split a coalition.

worked_example.title: Set the next move
worked_example.setup: Use the spectrum table to choose a realistic goal for each stakeholder.
steps: An active opponent: contain, or split from their allies.
A passive opponent: move to neutral.
A neutral: move to passive ally.
A passive ally: move to active, the highest-return move.
An active ally: organise and give them something to do.
worked_example.answer: Each group moves one step, with passive allies to active the best return.

mistakes: Mapping only who is in the game. Ask who is missing too.
Spending effort on active opponents. The winnable ground is the passive ally.
Leaving the map for a year. It will describe a configuration that has already moved.
Arguing against a caricature. Prepare for the opponent's strongest argument.

recall.q: What are the four roles on a stakeholder map?
recall.a: Targets, allies, opponents and influentials.

recall.q: Who is the target?
recall.a: Whoever can say yes, often a busy undecided official.

recall.q: What is the highest-return move on the spectrum?
recall.a: Moving a passive ally to active.

recall.q: What should a coalition settle early?
recall.a: The shared goal, who speaks, how decisions are made, whether members may act alone and what happens on a partial win.

recall.q: What does the matrix say to do with high influence and low support?
recall.a: Persuade them.

sections.title: Strategy & Theory of Change
sections.big_idea: Strategy is an argument about how change will happen. **If it cannot fail, it cannot be evaluated.**
in_plain_words: A strategy links goal, objectives, targets and tactics, and makes each specific: the district collector in place of 'the government', a recruitment notification by March in place of 'raise awareness'. Objectives should be SMART, but achievability depends on the target's power and deadlines belong to the political calendar.

A theory of change states the assumptions underneath each step. It maps from activities to outputs, outcomes and impact. Outputs are what you control, and outcomes are what others do because of you. Plan a primary route and a backup, match tactics to targets, be honest about resources, and **fit it on one page** with a review date.

key_terms.meaning: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
A testable account of how activities lead to change.
A step that must hold for the next to follow.
A route to the goal, with a backup if it stalls.
A condition set in advance for changing route.
What others do because of you.

worked_example.title: Test an objective against SMART
worked_example.setup: Compare two objectives from the deck.
steps: 'Raise awareness' names no decision, so it fails Specific and Measurable.
'Recruitment notification issued by March' names an act and a date.
It is measurable because a notification either exists or does not.
Achievable depends on whether the department can act without new law.
Relevant means it links to the root cause: vacant posts.
worked_example.answer: The notification objective passes SMART, while raising awareness fails every test.

mistakes: Writing a strategy that nothing could contradict. Name targets and dates.
Reporting outputs as outcomes. A coalition formed is not a changed behaviour.
Betting on one pathway. Plan a backup with a trigger.
Pitching a costless ask to the finance department. An ask without a costing does not survive it.

recall.q: What are the four elements of the strategy spine?
recall.a: Goal, objectives, targets and tactics.

recall.q: Which ToC assumption usually breaks?
recall.a: That the target has authority and the political cost of acting is bearable.

recall.q: Who controls activities, outputs, outcomes and impact?
recall.a: You control activities and outputs, others control outcomes because of you, and many actors share impact.

recall.q: What does the finance department respond to?
recall.a: Fiscal argument only.

recall.q: What goes on a one-page strategy?
recall.a: The goal, SMART objectives, targets and influentials, matched tactics, assumptions and indicators with a review date.

sections.title: The Policy Process & Windows
sections.big_idea: Policy changes when problem, policy and politics align. **Be ready, because windows close in weeks.**
in_plain_words: Evidence earns a hearing and politics decides. Kingdon's multiple-streams framework describes three streams: problems, policies and politics. They flow largely independently, and big change comes when they join in a policy window. Advocates control the first two and must read the third.

Windows open through focusing events, new ministers, budget and election cycles, court rulings and shifting mood. A policy entrepreneur has a costed solution drafted years early and delegated authority to move within days. Adoption is not the finish line: **the implementing rules are where wins are reversed**, so plan and fund the implementation fight from the start.

diagram.note: Kingdon: change happens when the three streams are joined

key_terms.meaning: Kingdon's model of problem, policy and politics streams.
The brief opening when the three streams align.
A disaster, scandal or crisis that draws attention.
Someone who couples a ready solution to a problem at a window.
Forcing an ignored issue into official attention.
Detailed rules that can narrow or reverse a law.

worked_example.title: Which stream is missing?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's stream table on three campaigns.
steps: Officials describe a condition as a plain fact: the problem stream is missing, so frame it as urgent.
A problem is named but nobody asks what should be done and you have no draft: the policy stream is missing, so cost a solution.
A new minister arrives and a budget is due: the politics stream is flowing, so be ready.
worked_example.answer: Frame the problem, ready a costed solution, and ride the politics stream.

mistakes: Believing the best evidence wins. Research that arrives after the window closed has no effect.
Handing over a position paper. Ready means draft text, a costing and an implementation route.
Using a disaster to manufacture urgency. Advancing a pre-existing solution is legitimate; manufacturing urgency is not.
Disbanding at adoption. Rules, funds and staffing decide delivery.

recall.q: What are Kingdon's three streams?
recall.a: Problem, policy and politics.

recall.q: What opens a policy window?
recall.a: A focusing event, a new government or minister, a budget or election cycle, a court ruling or shifting public mood.

recall.q: Which policy stages are most neglected?
recall.a: Formulation, implementation and evaluation.

recall.q: What is the most reliable route onto the agenda?
recall.a: New data nobody had, if credible and simple.

recall.q: Why do implementing rules matter?
recall.a: Rules can add conditions and make a progressive law inert, with little attention.

sections.title: Tactics & Messaging
sections.big_idea: Evidence earns the hearing and story moves people. **Keep the ask fixed** and flex the frame, messenger and channel.
in_plain_words: Persuasion needs evidence and narrative together. Evidence survives scrutiny and answers cost questions, narrative makes people act, and the order depends on audience: story first for the public, evidence first for officials. A message has four parts: problem, solution, action and why now. Why now converts agreement into action.

The messenger matters as much as the message. The affected person is often the most credible, with a technical expert for a sceptical ministry. Channels each have a strength and a failure point, and an online-only campaign excludes the unconnected. Coalitions and grassroots mobilisation add numbers. **A frame is a bridge**, and unusual allies show it works.

key_terms.meaning: The human story that makes people care.
The reason to act this month, the window or deadline.
The person delivering the message.
Unequal online access that skews who a campaign hears.
Organising people into countable pressure.
A frame that lets those who disagree elsewhere support this ask.

worked_example.title: One ask, four audiences
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's audience table. The core ask stays the same.
steps: Finance ministry: lead with cost, saving and fiscal risk.
Line department: lead with feasibility and workload.
Community: lead with dignity, entitlement and rights.
Editor: lead with a story that has a face and a number.
In every row the core ask is unchanged.

mistakes: Sending the same report to a ministry, a journalist and peers. It serves none.
Changing the ask by audience. The coalition then argues about what it wants.
Treating reach as pressure. Reach statistics measure people already inclined to agree.
Putting the NGO in front by default. The affected person is often more credible and carries risk.

recall.q: What are the four elements of a message?
recall.a: Problem, solution, action and why now.

recall.q: Which element is most often missing?
recall.a: Why now.

recall.q: Who is the most credible messenger to a sceptical ministry?
recall.a: A recognised technical expert.

recall.q: What does the digital divide do to an online-only campaign?
recall.a: It silently excludes women, the poor and rural communities.

recall.q: What is the signal that a frame is working?
recall.a: Unusual allies, such as a business association and a workers' union, back the same ask.

sections.title: Monitoring, Evaluation & Learning
sections.big_idea: Advocacy needs its own tools. **Claim contribution, record markers as they happen**, and learn from failed assumptions.
in_plain_words: Advocacy is hard to measure because change is slow and non-linear, many actors push, attribution is unclear and there is no counterfactual. The response is different tools, with documentation as the foundation. Track intermediate markers: changed language, a committee agenda, media using your framing, coalition growth, a public commitment.

Contribution analysis, outcome harvesting, process tracing and most significant change each answer a different question. All need contemporaneous records. Evaluate to learn: a wrong assumption found is a success if you act on it. **Report accurately to funders**, claiming contribution, including setbacks and showing the learning.

left.title: Attribution
items: Too many hands on the lever

right.title: Contribution
items: 'We plausibly helped, and here is how'

key_terms.meaning: A plausible, evidenced claim that you helped.
Identify observed changes, then work back to your role.
Trace the chain of events behind one decision.
Collect stories of change and judge what mattered.
What would have happened without you.
An early sign the theory of change is working.

worked_example.title: Which claims are defensible?
steps: 'We caused this policy change': almost never defensible.
'We contributed, and here is how': defensible with documented markers.
'The change would not have happened without us': rarely provable.
'We were one of several actors; our role was X': defensible, and more credible.
worked_example.answer: Prefer the second and fourth claims, which can be evidenced.

mistakes: Claiming sole credit. Allies and experienced funders can see who else was pushing.
Reconstructing markers later. An outcome recalled is an assertion, a dated document is a finding.
Using a service-delivery results framework. Outcome harvesting fits advocacy better.
Leaving reflection to goodwill. Schedule it.

recall.q: Name the four difficulties of measuring advocacy.
recall.a: Long and non-linear change, many actors, attribution and no counterfactual.

recall.q: What does outcome harvesting do?
recall.a: It identifies observable changes in actors' behaviour, then works back to whether and how the advocacy contributed.

recall.q: What should you record for each marker?
recall.a: The quote or document, the date and the source.

recall.q: Why is an unfulfilled commitment valuable?
recall.a: It is the strongest lever in the implementation fight, if the exact words were captured.

recall.q: What should a funder report say about credit?
recall.a: 'We contributed to', never 'we achieved'.

sections.title: Ethics, Risk & Sustainability
sections.big_idea: An advocate's power is legitimacy. **Be accountable downward**, protect people from harm and leave power behind.
in_plain_words: Legitimacy rests on mandate, proximity, accountability and track record. The practical test is to read your ask back to the community. Accountability runs first to constituents, then to funders and government, and the community must win when priorities diverge. Do no harm means weighing risks with the community, since speaking out can expose people.

The operating environment is tight: civic space has narrowed, and India's FCRA bars sub-granting and affects who can fund advocacy. Evidence integrity is non-negotiable. Sustainability means leaving behind an organised constituency, local leadership, independent funding, institutional memory and defended implementation. **A win unwatched can be reversed.**

key_terms.meaning: A credible claim to represent or serve those affected.
Answering first to the people you claim to represent.
Weighing risks to constituents before acting.
India's law governing NGOs' access to foreign funds.
The room civil society has to organise and dissent.
A position written down in advance that you will not trade.

worked_example.title: Strong or weak legitimacy?
worked_example.setup: Apply the deck's four legitimacy questions to an organisation's answers.
steps: 'We work in this sector' is a weak answer to who authorised you.
'A community body asked us to' is a strong answer.
'Our board' is a weak answer to who holds you to account.
'The people we claim to represent' is the strong answer.
Finally, ask whether they would recognise the ask: 'they wrote it' is the strongest answer.
worked_example.answer: Strong answers name the community as the source of mandate, accountability and the ask.

mistakes: Putting a photograph and village name in a case study. It can identify someone permanently.
Waiting to be caught on an error. Correct it first and visibly.
Pretending foreign funding carries no risk. Plan around it.
Celebrating a win and leaving. Rules get amended and budget lines lapse.

recall.q: What is the first accountability of an advocacy organisation?
recall.a: Downward, to the people it claims to represent.

recall.q: What did the 2020 FCRA amendments do?
recall.a: Barred sub-granting of foreign funds and raised the compliance burden.

recall.q: What risks can a campaign create for constituents?
recall.a: Loss of work, local retaliation, state attention, social exclusion and exposure through photographs and names.

recall.q: What are the four honesty rules?
recall.a: Never fabricate, never cherry-pick, acknowledge uncertainty, correct errors fast.

recall.q: What is the deepest test of sustainability?
recall.a: What the community can do next year without you.

notes.2: Eleven sections build one argument: what advocacy is, its approaches, power, the cycle, framing, mapping, strategy, the policy process, tactics, measurement and ethics. **Read the power section before the strategy section**, because a plan written without a power analysis pushes on the wrong door.
notes.4: Advocacy asks why a need exists and who can change it, while service delivery asks how to meet the need. Both are legitimate and lead to different organisations. The slide ends with a warning: **advocacy needs its own strategy, timeline and indicators**. Treating it as something communications does after the programme is the common mistake.
notes.5: Advocacy has four targets: policy, practice, power and norms, with timeframes from years to a generation. Most campaigns win at policy and stall at practice, so **adoption and implementation are separate fights**. Norms work is slowest and least fundable, yet it makes the other three last.
notes.6: The table sets two kinds of work side by side. Service delivery fills the gap and counts people reached, while advocacy closes the gap at source and counts rules changed. Shared attribution, political risk and **outputs that are hard to count** explain why advocacy is underfunded. Avoid running it on quarterly reporting cycles.
notes.7: This is the case for pairing the two kinds of work. An NGO running 50 schools well reaches a few thousand children, while 5,000 government schools lack teachers and only a policy and budget shift reaches them. **Run the model, document it, then use it as evidence** for a policy ask.
notes.8: Four words get used as synonyms. Advocacy is the umbrella, lobbying a narrow tactic aimed at legislators, campaigning a sustained public push, and activism visible, often confrontational action. Choose your words carefully because lobbying can be regulated elsewhere. **In India the sharper constraint is charitable and foreign-funding status.**
notes.9: Lobbying means direct, private communication about a specific bill, rule or budget line. Advocacy also covers norms, public opinion, courts and years of agenda-setting before any decision moment exists. Using lobbying as the name of the whole field invites compliance trouble, so **call campaigning by its own name**.
notes.10: Five kinds of actor, each with a strength and a gap: communities bring legitimacy, NGOs reach and evidence, coalitions numbers, researchers and media credibility, insiders timing. None has everything, which is **the structural case for coalitions**. Protect insiders: never name them and never use them for a quick win.
notes.12: Insider advocacy trades access for the risk of co-option, and outsider advocacy trades independence for the risk of being shut out. The best campaigns run both, often through different organisations. The insider failure mode is subtle: **being in the room is not influence**, and the invitation itself can be the concession.
notes.13: Four approaches: lobbying, campaigning, litigation and mobilisation. Read the table as a trade-off between speed and durability. Lobbying is fastest and easiest to reverse, mobilisation slowest and most durable. The slide advises sequencing: **mobilise, campaign, lobby, then litigate when the route shuts**.
notes.14: PIL lets citizens ask courts to enforce rights for those who cannot reach them, and it has shaped food, education and environment rights in India. A judgment starts an implementation fight. Use litigation when the political route is closed, because **filing first forecloses the cheaper options**.
notes.15: A jan sunwai reads official records aloud in the village, so the people named can answer or fail to. Public verification is what separates a social audit from an allegation. The slide notes that social audit became statutory under MGNREGA and survives in the VB-G RAM G Act, though **quality varies enormously by state**.
notes.16: MKSS in Rajasthan is the sequence to learn: organise workers over unpaid wages, read muster rolls in public, document discrepancies, campaign for a right to information, and win the 2005 RTI Act. A **local grievance became a national right** over roughly a decade, and nothing in it started as a legislative campaign.
notes.17: Advocacy WITH puts affected people in charge of the agenda and the speaking. Advocacy FOR speaks on their behalf. Default to WITH. The fourth row is the honest test: **what can the community do next year that it could not do last year?** If the answer is nothing, the campaign built power for the organisation.
notes.18: Before you speak, ask who gave you a mandate, whether affected people would recognise your ask, whether any are in the room and who reports back to them. Having no mandate is workable if you say so plainly. **Implying a representativeness you lack is what damages credibility.**
notes.19: There is no single right approach. Match it to the target, your power, the risk and the moment. The question organisations skip is who bears the consequence, you or your constituents. Then sequence: evidence first, **quiet engagement, public pressure, litigation**, each step keeping the next option open.
notes.21: Every advocacy problem is a question of power. Four wrong assumptions cost months, and the commonest is that **the target has authority they lack**. Test early with a small ask: if the target cannot deliver something minor within their stated remit, the main ask will fail too.
notes.22: Lukes gives three faces of power: winning open decisions, keeping issues off the table, and shaping what people want and accept. Diagnose the face before choosing a tactic, because **a lobbying strategy is wasted on a second-face problem**. There is no meeting at which to lobby.
notes.23: Match the symptom to the face. A lost vote is the first face, no meeting or hearing is the second, and affected people seeing no problem is the third. The third face is slowest and least fundable, but **naming it is itself advocacy**. Campaigns that skip it have no constituency when a window opens.
notes.24: Four expressions of power. Only power over is zero-sum, and it is what you seek to change. Power with, power to and power within grow when used. **Advocacy converts power within and power to into power with** to confront power over. Power within is the precondition and the hardest to measure.
notes.25: Ask what power your work creates. A campaign can win a policy and leave the community unorganised, or lose a policy and leave it organised. The middle row of the table is a real result: an organised community is positioned to win next time. **Funder reports that count only wins distort practice.**
notes.26: Gaventa's cube has three axes: spaces (closed, invited, claimed), places (local, national, global) and forms (visible, hidden, invisible). **Use it to ask where a decision happens, at what level and which power operates.** Forms map onto Lukes: visible is the first face, hidden the second, invisible the third.
notes.27: Read all three axes of the cube before you choose a tactic. The slide's example: closed space with invisible power points to RTI and consciousness-raising first. **The commonest error is a tactic for an invited space** when the decision is made in a closed one.
notes.28: Closed spaces need prising open, invited spaces need preparation, and claimed spaces need building and defending. The trap in invited spaces is tokenism: consulted, then ignored. **Test an invited space by asking what changed after the last one.** If nothing changed, treat the invitation as public relations.
notes.30: Advocacy is a loop of research, strategy, action, monitoring and learning, and it loops because the political world moves. The table shows what skipping each stage costs. The slide's diagnosis is that **failures are usually strategy failures**: real energy aimed at a target who cannot deliver.
notes.31: Research means two kinds of homework: evidence about the problem and power analysis about the decision. The fourth row, what has been tried, is cheapest and most skipped. **Knowing why the last attempt failed is worth more than new data**, and power research needs people who read budgets and rules of business.
notes.32: Strategy turns analysis into a plan: an objective, targets, tactics and a theory of change. Compare the weak answers in the table with the questions. Each weak answer is vague about an actor. **If you cannot name the person who signs, you do not yet have a strategy.**
notes.33: Action is the visible phase, but its success was decided earlier. Each row names a precondition: roles agreed before the coalition acts, evidence written for the target, a specific ask for the meeting, a solution drafted before a window opens. **Package evidence for the reader you want**: ministry, journalist or peers.
notes.34: Track signals along the way: a minister using your framing, a consultation, an opponent responding, an unusual ally, a tagged budget line. **An opponent's public response is the most reliable early signal.** Record each marker as it happens, dated and with evidence, because later reconstruction is unverifiable.
notes.35: After each cycle ask what moved, whether the target had the power you assumed, which assumption failed and what opponents did. A failed assumption found early is the most valuable output of a cycle. It rarely appears in reports because it reads as failure, so **put it into the next strategy**.
notes.36: RTI took about a decade to reach statute, MGNREGA needed years of campaign and drafting, and the Right to Education years including a constitutional amendment. Expect a marathon. **Endurance is an organisational property**: documented institutional memory, leadership beyond one person and a constituency that stays organised between pushes.
notes.38: A problem is broad and an issue is actionable. 'Child malnutrition' becomes 'the district must fill 200 vacant anganwadi posts'. **The test is whether a named decision-maker can grant the ask.** A campaign is a sequence of issues carved from one problem, and winning data first can make the next issue possible.
notes.39: Keep asking 'but why?' until you reach a rule someone can change. In the example, malnutrition leads to non-functioning anganwadis, then vacant posts and delayed funds, then recruitment rules and treasury release. **Stop at the rule someone can change.** Transparency asks, such as publishing release dates, are often cheaper to win.
notes.40: The problem tree puts effects as branches, the core problem as the trunk and causes as roots. **Frame from the branches and aim at the roots**: stunting moves people, but vacant posts and delayed funds are what a district collector can change. Build the tree with the affected community.
notes.41: An ask is a concrete action for a named decision-maker. The table gives five tests: specific, winnable, timebound, attributable and meaningful. The last two pull against each other. **Write the ask as the sentence you want the official to say yes to.** If it takes a paragraph, it is several asks.
notes.42: Too ambitious an ask gets no engagement, and too modest an ask is granted at once and changes nothing. The right calibration is an official who engages and says it is difficult. **Aim for a stretch but credible ask**, and sequence a winnable first ask before a harder one to build the credibility the harder one needs.
notes.43: The same facts framed as dignity, public health, cost saving or safety reach different audiences. The frame decides which department owns the issue and so which budget it can come from. **Run several frames only through different messengers**, as a coalition, or one organisation looks incoherent.
notes.44: The shift from need to right turns a beneficiary into a claimant with somewhere to go when refused. The Right to Food, Right to Education and Right to Information campaigns all made this move. Weigh the cost the slide names: rights framing can **antagonise governments** that would have cooperated, and it needs an enforcement route.
notes.45: Framing chooses emphasis and must never distort the facts. The slide's test is whether your framing would survive a public fact-check by your opponent. **Omitting inconvenient context is where framing turns into distortion**, along with striking numbers stripped of caveats. Credibility is the one asset you cannot rebuild quickly.
notes.47: Map before you choose tactics. The table links each question to a decision: who grants the ask is your target, who influences them is your route, who shares the goal is your coalition. **Ask who is affected but absent**, the question maps omit. Redo the map each cycle.
notes.48: Four roles: targets, allies, opponents and influentials, plus absent voices. The target is whoever can say yes, often a busy undecided official. **Influentials are the most underused category**, since targets change position because someone they trust raised the issue. People swap roles, so today's influential can be tomorrow's target.
notes.49: Lakey's spectrum runs from active allies to active opponents, and you rarely convert opponents. **The highest-return move is turning a passive ally into an active one**, someone who agrees and does nothing. Each group needs a different ask: tasks for active allies, a low-cost first action for passive ones.
notes.50: Plot each stakeholder by influence and support. High influence with high support is a partner, and high influence with low support is someone to persuade. **Most campaigns over-invest in the already convinced.** Influence depends on the issue: the junior official who drafts the note may outweigh a powerful general figure.
notes.51: This illustrative map highlights the amber stakeholders: high influence and undecided. **Winning a few of them often decides the campaign.** Draw your own map with names and positions, mark the amber ones, then decide who approaches each, using the influentials around them.
notes.52: Study your opponents instead of demonising them: their interests, strongest argument, internal splits and what they would accept. **Prepare a rebuttal to their best argument.** Demonising forecloses the deal, and today's opponent is frequently needed as an ally on the next issue.
notes.53: Allies multiply power only when coordinated. Settle five things early: the shared goal, who speaks, how decisions are made, whether members may act alone, and **what happens on a partial win**, the most common breaking point. Let members keep their own identity around a common core ask.
notes.55: Strategy is a coherent argument about how change will happen. The table contrasts weak and strong versions of goal, objective, target and tactic. Weak versions sound like advocacy and cannot fail. **A strategy that cannot fail cannot be evaluated.** Name the district collector, since 'the government' cannot say yes.
notes.56: SMART objectives get an advocacy twist. Achievability depends on the target's power, and deadlines belong to the political calendar: budget, session and election dates. 'Raise awareness' fails every SMART test. **Name the decision the awareness is meant to produce.**
notes.57: A theory of change is an explicit, testable account of how activities lead to change, including assumptions. Read the chain: publish evidence, someone reads it, finds it credible, has authority, can bear the cost, then acts. **The fourth assumption usually breaks**: targets agree privately and do nothing. List assumptions in a separate column.
notes.58: Activities and outputs are yours to control, outcomes are what others do because of you, and impact belongs to many actors. **Advocacy success lives at the outcome level**, which is why it is hard to fund, report and evaluate. Report a coalition formed or a report published as outputs.
notes.59: Plan a primary route and a backup, each with a trigger for switching. The example is insider negotiation, then public pressure after two missed commitments. **Decide the switching trigger in advance**, because sunk cost and friendships make abandoning a stalled insider track feel like betrayal.
notes.60: Match the tactic to the target. A senior bureaucrat responds to evidence, costing and quiet meetings, the public to story, and the finance department to fiscal argument only. **The finance row decides the most outcomes**: an ask without a costing does not survive it. Mismatching is advocacy's commonest waste.
notes.61: Be honest about what you can sustain. Each resource carries a hard question: who does this when the lead leaves, can we fund three more years or one, are relationships the organisation's or one person's. **Match ambition to what survives the first setback.**
notes.62: A one-page strategy holds the goal, two or three dated SMART objectives, named targets and influentials, tactics per target, and assumptions and indicators with a review date. **If it does not fit on a page, the thinking is unfinished.** Set the review date when you write it.
notes.64: Policy rarely changes on merit alone. Evidence earns a hearing and politics decides. Kingdon's multiple streams say problem, policy and politics must join in a window. **You can seldom create a window but you can be ready for one**: have the solution drafted before you need it.
notes.65: Five stages: agenda-setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation. The table marks formulation, implementation and evaluation as neglected. **Formulation decides what the policy says and implementation decides whether it happens.** Treat the model as a checklist of where advocacy has work to do.
notes.66: Kingdon's three streams flow separately: problems, policies and politics. Big change comes when they join. **Only the first two are in your control**, and advocates neglect the policy stream. Ready means draft text, a costing, an implementation route and answers to the finance department's three objections.
notes.67: The picture shows three streams meeting in a policy window, where an advocate who is ready wins. Windows close fast. **Preparation is the whole game**: a polished solution, a warm coalition and relationships already built, because the window is too short to build them.
notes.68: Windows open through focusing events, a new government or minister, budget or election cycles, court rulings and shifting public mood. Every row is preparation: briefing ready for day one, the ask already written. **Windows close in weeks.** Do not manufacture urgency from someone's tragedy.
notes.69: A policy entrepreneur couples a ready solution to a recognised problem when a window opens. Their edge is preparation: a costed solution, relationships, credibility and the ability to move within days. **That last item is organisational.** If the board must convene to respond, you miss the window, so delegate authority in advance.
notes.70: Most issues never reach a debate, which is Lukes' second face. Routes onto the agenda: media with a face and a number, striking new data, a focusing event, litigation, an insider. **New data is the most reliable route and the most within your control**, if it is defensible and easy to repeat.
notes.71: A law on paper changes nothing until it is funded, staffed and enforced. After adoption the fight moves to funding, staffing, implementing rules, awareness and grievance routes. **Implementing rules are where wins are reversed**, because rule-making draws less attention than legislation. Plan and fund this fight from the start.
notes.73: Evidence earns a hearing and survives scrutiny, and narrative makes people act. In the table only 'both' scores yes on every row. **Sequence by audience**: story first for the public and press, evidence first for officials and finance departments. The content is the same and the order decides whether you are heard.
notes.74: A message has four parts: problem, solution, action and why now. **Why now is the element most often missing**, and it turns agreement into action, since without a reason to act this month a sympathetic official can defer at no cost. One message repeated identically by every member beats clever variants.
notes.75: Keep the ask fixed and flex the framing: cost for a finance ministry, feasibility for a line department, dignity for a community, a face and a number for an editor. **The right-hand column is the discipline.** If the ask varies by audience, the coalition starts arguing about what it wants.
notes.76: Pick the messenger for the audience: a technical expert for a sceptical ministry, the affected person for the public, a trusted local figure for a community. The NGO is rarely the best messenger. **Speaking publicly carries risk**, so prepare people, agree what they will not be asked and plan for backlash.
notes.77: Each channel has a strength and a failure point. Media gives legitimacy but not control of the framing, digital gives speed but reaches your own bubble, grassroots gives depth but is slow. **An online-only campaign silently excludes women, the poor and rural communities.** Reach statistics do not measure pressure.
notes.78: Coalitions that hold agree a goal and message early, define roles and decide transparently. Unusual allies matter most: **a business body and a workers' union backing the same ask** removes the easy way to dismiss it. Most collapses are about process, such as who spoke, more than about the goal.
notes.79: Mobilisation turns numbers into pressure and also builds legitimacy, power with and power within. The middle rows explain why it is worth its cost even when it loses: **the campaign ends but an organised constituency does not**. Keep turnout claims real and verifiable, since inflated numbers cost credibility.
notes.80: A good frame is a bridge that lets people who disagree with you elsewhere support this ask. Narrow partisan frames energise your base and close doors, while broad values-based frames let unlikely allies join. **Unusual allies are the strongest sign that a frame is working.**
notes.82: Four difficulties make advocacy hard to measure: long and non-linear change, many actors, attribution and no counterfactual. The honest responses are intermediate markers, contribution claims, contribution analysis or process tracing, and a **documented causal chain**. None of the difficulties is an excuse for skipping evaluation.
notes.83: Claim contribution. Attribution ('we caused this') is almost never provable, while contribution ('we plausibly helped, and here is how') is defensible. **Agree in advance how credit will be described**, since attribution disputes damage coalitions after wins more often than disagreements do during campaigns.
notes.84: Track markers along the way: a decision-maker's changed language, an agenda item, media using your framing, coalition growth, a commitment. **Record each with its evidence at the time**: quote, date, source. An unfulfilled public commitment is the strongest lever in the implementation fight, but only with the exact words.
notes.85: Outcome harvesting starts from observed changes in actors' behaviour and works backwards to ask whether and how you contributed. It suits advocacy because **you cannot predict which change will come, but you can recognise and trace it** once it does. Use it when results are unpredictable.
notes.86: Four methods: outcome harvesting, contribution analysis, process tracing and most significant change. Match each to a question: what changed, is our causal story plausible, did our action move this decision, what mattered to whom. **All four need contemporaneous documentation**, so the method is decided years in advance.
notes.87: Evaluate to learn as well as to report. A wrong assumption found is a success if you act on it. The table lists what enables learning: a written theory of change, assumptions listed separately, **a scheduled review** and documentation that outlives staff. Schedule the reflection, because a live campaign will not find time for it.
notes.88: This illustrative chart shows intermediate outcomes accumulating for years before the year 5 policy win. Use it to explain to your team and funders **why invisible progress counts**. Tracking markers keeps a long campaign motivated and accountable while the headline outcome is out of reach.
notes.89: Report contribution, intermediate outcomes, setbacks and learning. Write 'we contributed to' wherever you would be tempted to write 'we achieved', and show what failed and what you changed. **Over-claiming is the fastest way to lose an experienced funder**, who can usually see who else was pushing.
notes.91: Legitimacy rests on mandate, proximity, accountability and track record. The table contrasts weak and strong answers to each. **Read your ask back to the community**: if it surprises them, the mandate is missing. Opponents attack legitimacy first, and once it falls, evidence and access weaken together.
notes.92: Advocacy organisations feel pulls from funders, constituents, government relationships and survival. The anchor is downward accountability to the people you claim to represent. **Write your non-negotiables down before the pressure arrives**, because deciding what you will not trade is easier before a specific offer exists.
notes.93: Speaking out can expose people to backlash from employers, local power-holders or the state, and the campaign itself can expose them through photographs, names and case studies. **Weigh the risks with the community**, who bear the consequence. Sometimes quiet advocacy or protected identities is the ethical choice.
notes.94: Civic space across the region has narrowed through tighter regulation, funding restrictions, surveillance and costlier protest. Treat this as the operating environment. Adaptations that work: diversified domestic funding, coalition structures that spread exposure, scrupulous compliance and **tactics chosen with constituent risk explicitly weighed**.
notes.95: FCRA governs foreign funds. The 2020 amendments barred sub-granting and raised the compliance burden, and the Act has been used against advocacy groups. **An organisation dependent on foreign funding for advocacy carries a specific, known risk.** Rules change, so check the current ones before you plan.
notes.96: Never fabricate, cherry-pick or exaggerate, and correct mistakes openly and quickly. **Publish your own correction before an opponent finds the error.** Acknowledging uncertainty gains credibility with officials and journalists, who trust sources that mark their own limits.
notes.97: The deepest measure of advocacy is power redistributed. What outlasts a campaign: an organised constituency, local leadership, independent funding, institutional memory and defended implementation. **Ask what the community can do next year without you.** A win unwatched can be reversed through amended rules and lapsed budget lines.
notes.98: Four texts: VeneKlasen and Miller for planning, Lukes for the three faces, Kingdon for streams and windows, Gaventa for the power cube. The slide also lists Oxfam and ODI guides and three ImpactMojo courses. **Start with VeneKlasen and Miller** if you are planning a campaign this quarter.
notes.99: Five takeaways, each preventing a specific failure: analyse power first, choose a specific ask, map stakeholders, be ready for the window, and advocate with people. Four of the five happen before any public activity. **If you keep one habit, name the person who signs.**
